title: Nucleotides, DNA and RNA structure; Amino acids and peptide bonds
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM07#t4 term and clue written for the game; BM07#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM10b#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM10b#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM07#N.2b, BM10b#N.15, BM07#N.4b, BM07#N.6b, BM07#N.13.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Polypeptide
items.clue: Many protein monomers joined in one chain

items.label: Amino acids
items.clue: The monomers of proteins, each built around a central carbon atom

items.label: Base sequence
items.clue: The order of A, C, G and T along a strand: this is the information

items.label: Messenger RNA
items.clue: Copy of a gene made by complementary pairing in which A pairs with U

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the R groups of amino acids?

options.text: They are the same in every amino acid, which differ instead in their amine and carboxyl groups.
They form the covalent bonds that join each amino acid to the next one in the chain.
They are nitrogenous bases that pair with one another to hold the chain in its shape.
They differ among amino acids, and their chemical properties affect how the chain folds.

questions.explanation: The R group is the only part that differs. Whether it is nonpolar, polar or ionic decides which interactions it forms, and so how that region of the protein folds.

questions.stem: Two DNA molecules from two hypothetical species of bacteria each contain the same number of nucleotides, and in both, 30% of the bases are adenine, 30% thymine, 20% guanine and 20% cytosine. The two molecules carry different genetic information. Which statement best explains how this is possible?

options.text: The amino acids attached along their strands are arranged in a different order in each.
The nucleotides of each species are built around a different five-carbon sugar.
Each molecule is folded into a different three-dimensional shape that stores information.
Their nucleotides are arranged in a different order along each molecule.

questions.stem: During protein synthesis, a free amino acid is joined to the end of a growing polypeptide. Which statement correctly describes how the amino acid becomes part of the polypeptide?

options.text: A water molecule is added between it and the end of the chain, joining the two together.
The chain's last carboxyl group forms a covalent bond with the amino acid's amine group, releasing water.
Its R group forms a covalent bond with the R group of the amino acid at the end of the chain.
Its amine group is held to the carboxyl group at the end of the chain by a hydrogen bond.

questions.stem: A polypeptide of 150 amino acids is assembled by dehydration synthesis. How does the number of water molecules change as the whole chain is formed?

options.text: 150 released
298 released
149 released
149 consumed

questions.explanation: Each peptide bond releases one water molecule. A chain of 150 needs 149 bonds: 149 water molecules.

questions.stem: Two short polypeptides, P and Q, are each made of the same five amino acids, but the amino acids are joined in a different order in P and in Q. Which statement about P and Q is correct?

options.text: They are the same molecule, because they contain exactly the same amino acids.
They have the same properties, because a polypeptide's properties come from its amine and carboxyl groups.
They are different polypeptides, because their R groups sit in different positions along the chain.
They are different polypeptides, because their peptide bonds join different pairs of R groups.

questions.explanation: Each chain has four peptide bonds and the same backbone, but the R groups are in a different order. Order is one of the three sources of variety, with chain length and repeats.
